details: PHP runs on the server; the browser only receives the HTML output.
You can embed PHP inside an HTML page using `<?php ... ?>` tags.
`echo` prints text (or variables) into the response body.
Most statements end with `;` and PHP files typically use the `.php` extension.
If you can see PHP code in the browser, the server is not executing PHP (it is serving the file as plain text).
summary: PHP is server-side (your source code stays on the server).

details: Variables always start with `$` and are created when you first assign to them.
PHP is dynamically typed: the same variable can hold a string, number, array, etc.
Statements usually end with `;` and blocks are wrapped with `{ ... }`.
Use `var_dump($value)` while learning to inspect types and values.
Prefer meaningful variable names and keep naming consistent (`$userEmail`, `$total`...).
Single quotes (`'...'`) are literal: variables are not expanded.
Double quotes (`"..."`) interpolate variables and support escape sequences like `\n`.
Concatenate strings with `.` (dot), not `+`.
Common helpers: `strlen`, `substr`, `str_replace`, `trim`.
When outputting user input, escape with `htmlspecialchars` to avoid XSS.
summary: Double quotes interpolate; single quotes are literal.

details: PHP arrays are ordered maps: they can be indexed (`[0, 1, 2]`) or associative (`['k' => 'v']`).
Access elements with `$arr[$key]` and check existence with `isset($arr[$key])`.
Iterate using `foreach ($arr as $value)` or `foreach ($arr as $key => $value)`.
Useful functions: `count`, `array_merge`, `array_map`, `array_filter`, `in_array`.
Prefer associative arrays for structured data and keep keys consistent.
summary: Arrays can be indexed or associative.

details: Use `if / elseif / else` for branching and `switch` for discrete values.
Understand comparison: `==` coerces types; `===` compares type + value (recommended).
The ternary operator `cond ? a : b` is useful for simple decisions.
The null coalescing operator `??` provides defaults (`$x = $value ?? 'default';`).
Keep conditions readable; extract complex checks into well-named variables.
summary: Use ternary for simple inline decisions.

details: `for` is best when you know how many times to loop (counter-based).
`while` runs while a condition is true; `do ... while` runs at least once.
`foreach` is the go-to loop for arrays and iterable data.
Use `break` to exit a loop and `continue` to skip to the next iteration.
Avoid infinite loops by making sure the loop condition can become false.
Functions are declared with `function name($arg) { ... }`.
Return values using `return` (a function without `return` returns `null`).
You can set default arguments (`function f($x = 10) { ... }`).
Type hints (`string`, `int`, `array`, `User`) improve clarity and catch bugs earlier.
Anonymous functions and arrow functions are common for callbacks (arrays, collections).
summary: Use defaults and type hints for clarity.

details: Variables inside a function are local to that function by default.
Use `global $var;` or `$GLOBALS['var']` to access a global variable (avoid when possible).
`static` variables inside a function keep their value between calls.
Superglobals like `$_GET` and `$_POST` are available in any scope.
Prefer passing values into functions instead of relying on globals.
summary: Function scope is local by default.

details: `include` emits a warning on failure; `require` throws a fatal error (stops execution).
Use `include_once` / `require_once` to avoid loading the same file twice.
Build reliable paths using `__DIR__` (e.g., `require __DIR__ . '/lib.php';`).
Prefer `require` for critical application files (config, autoloader).
In modern projects, Composer autoloading replaces most manual includes.
Read form input from `$_POST` (POST) and `$_GET` (query string).
Never trust client input: validate types/format and enforce allowed values.
Escape output with `htmlspecialchars` when rendering user-provided values.
Use CSRF tokens for state-changing forms (POST/PUT/DELETE).
Return helpful error messages and keep validation logic close to input parsing.
Call `session_start()` before reading or writing `$_SESSION`.
Sessions store data server-side and identify the user via a session cookie.
Regenerate session IDs after login (`session_regenerate_id(true)`) to prevent fixation.
Store minimal session data (IDs/flags), not large objects.
Configure secure cookie flags when possible (`httponly`, `secure`, `samesite`).
summary: Sessions are server-side state tied to a cookie.
Keep session data small and secure.

details: `setcookie()` must run before any output is sent (headers first).
Cookies are stored in the browser and read via `$_COOKIE` on later requests.
Use expiration, path, domain and `SameSite` to control cookie behavior.
Use `HttpOnly` to reduce XSS impact and `Secure` over HTTPS.
Do not store secrets in cookies; store opaque IDs and validate server-side.
summary: Avoid storing sensitive data in cookies.

details: Classes bundle state (properties) and behavior (methods).
Visibility (`public`, `protected`, `private`) controls access to members.
Create objects using `new ClassName()` and access members with `->`.
`$this` refers to the current object inside a method.
Use OOP to model domain concepts (User, Order, Invoice) and keep logic organized.
`__construct()` runs automatically when an object is created.
Constructors set required state and validate inputs early.
In inheritance, call the parent constructor with `parent::__construct()` when needed.
Prefer explicit dependencies in constructors instead of creating objects inside methods.
Consider `readonly` properties (PHP 8.1+) for immutable value objects.
summary: Prefer dependency injection via constructor args.

details: Inheritance lets a class reuse behavior from a base class using `extends`.
Override methods to specialize behavior; call base logic with `parent::method()`.
Use `final` to prevent extending/overriding where it must stay fixed.
Use abstract base classes for shared templates (common properties and required methods).
Prefer composition (having another object) when inheritance becomes complicated.
summary: Prefer composition when inheritance is awkward.

details: Interfaces define a contract: method signatures without implementation.
A class uses `implements` to promise it provides those methods.
Interfaces enable polymorphism (swap implementations without changing callers).
A class can implement multiple interfaces.
Type-hint interfaces in function params to keep code flexible.
summary: One class can implement multiple interfaces.

details: Traits are a mechanism for horizontal code reuse across unrelated classes.
Include a trait with `use TraitName;` inside a class.
Resolve naming conflicts using `insteadof` and rename methods using `as`.
Use traits for small, focused behavior (logging helpers, timestamps).
Avoid turning traits into large grab-bags; keep them cohesive.
Namespaces prevent name collisions across large codebases.
Declare a namespace at the top of the file: `namespace App;`.
Import classes/functions with `use` statements.
Use fully qualified names when needed (`\App\User`).
Namespaces work best together with PSR-4 autoloading via Composer.
summary: Namespaces organize code and avoid collisions.

details: `composer.json` declares dependencies under `require` and `require-dev`.
`composer install` installs versions pinned in `composer.lock`.
`composer update` updates dependencies and rewrites `composer.lock`.
Libraries are installed into the `vendor/` directory.
You typically include `vendor/autoload.php` to enable autoloading.
Autoloading loads classes automatically when they are referenced.
PSR-4 maps namespaces to directories (configured in `composer.json`).
Run `composer dump-autoload` after changing autoload rules.
Always commit `composer.lock` for consistent installs across environments.
For production, consider optimized autoload (`--optimize-autoloader`).
Exceptions represent error conditions that should be handled explicitly.
Throw with `throw new Exception('message');` (or a more specific exception type).
Handle with `try { ... } catch (Exception $e) { ... } finally { ... }`.
Catch the most specific exception types first.
Do not swallow exceptions silently; log or return meaningful errors.
Read files with `file_get_contents()` and write files with `file_put_contents()`.
Use `fopen/fgets/fwrite` for streaming large files.
Always handle failure cases (missing file, permission errors).
Build safe paths with `__DIR__` and avoid user-controlled path concatenation.
When accepting filenames from users, validate and restrict to allowed directories.
Use `DateTime` or `DateTimeImmutable` instead of manually parsing timestamps.
Always be explicit about time zones (`new DateTime('now', new DateTimeZone('UTC'))`).
Format output with `$dt->format('Y-m-d H:i:s')`.
Compute differences using `$a->diff($b)` (returns a `DateInterval`).
Store timestamps in UTC and convert for display at the edges.
summary: Store times in UTC when possible.

details: `json_encode()` converts arrays/objects into JSON strings.
`json_decode()` parses JSON; pass `true` to get associative arrays.
Check encoding/decoding errors with `json_last_error()` and `json_last_error_msg()`.
Use `JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE` and `JSON_PRETTY_PRINT` during development if helpful.
Validate incoming JSON structure before trusting it.
summary: Use associative mode (`true`) if you want arrays.
Validate JSON structure before using it.

details: HTTP is request/response: method + URL + headers + body.
Read request info from `$_SERVER` (method, path, headers).
Set headers with `header('Name: value')` before output.
Redirect with `header('Location: /path', true, 302); exit;`.
Use meaningful status codes (200 OK, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error).
summary: HTTP requests include method, headers, and body.
Use correct status codes and redirects.

details: PDO is a database abstraction layer that supports multiple drivers.
Use prepared statements (`prepare` + `execute`) to prevent SQL injection.
Enable exceptions with `PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION`.
Use transactions for multi-step operations (`beginTransaction/commit/rollBack`).
Choose fetch modes (`FETCH_ASSOC`) for predictable data structures.
summary: PDO is a generic DB API.

details: MySQLi is a MySQL-specific API (procedural or object-oriented style).
It supports prepared statements similar to PDO.
If you only target MySQL, MySQLi is fine; for portability, prefer PDO.
Always handle connection errors and query errors explicitly.
Avoid building SQL with string concatenation; bind parameters instead.
summary: Use prepared statements and parameter binding.
Prefer PDO if you need portability.

details: cURL lets PHP make HTTP requests to other services.
Typical flow: `curl_init`, `curl_setopt`, `curl_exec`, `curl_close`.
Set headers, timeouts, and HTTP method via options.
Check errors using `curl_errno` and `curl_error`.
Do not disable SSL verification in production; fix certificates instead.
summary: Keep SSL verification enabled in production.

details: Regex is useful for matching and transforming text patterns.
Use `preg_match` to test/collect matches and `preg_replace` to replace patterns.
Patterns use delimiters (commonly `/.../`) and can include flags like `i` (case-insensitive).
Capture groups with parentheses and reference them in replacements if needed.
Prefer simpler string functions when possible; regex can become hard to maintain.
summary: Learn delimiters, flags, and capture groups.
Avoid overly complex regex when simpler code works.

details: Common web risks: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, and insecure password storage.
Use prepared statements (PDO/MySQLi) for database queries.
Escape output with `htmlspecialchars` when rendering untrusted data into HTML.
Hash passwords using `password_hash` and verify with `password_verify`.
Use least privilege: DB users should have only the permissions they need.
summary: Use prepared statements to prevent SQL injection.

details: Uploads arrive via `$_FILES` when a form uses `enctype='multipart/form-data'`.
Always validate file size, extension, and MIME type (server-side).
Move files with `move_uploaded_file()` to a safe location.
Store uploads outside the web root when possible and serve them through controlled routes.
Generate unique filenames to avoid overwriting and path traversal issues.
summary: Store safely (unique names, outside web root when possible).

details: `mail()` exists but is often unreliable and hard to configure across servers.
Prefer an SMTP library like PHPMailer or Symfony Mailer for real apps.
Use proper From/Reply-To headers and avoid user-controlled header values.
Send both HTML and plain-text versions when possible.
Log delivery failures and retry where appropriate.
PHPUnit is the standard unit testing framework for PHP.
Tests are regular PHP classes with methods that contain assertions.
Follow Arrange → Act → Assert for readable tests.
Keep tests fast; mock slow dependencies (network, database) when needed.
Run tests frequently and integrate into CI for reliability.
Frameworks (Laravel, Symfony) provide routing, controllers, templating, and tooling.
Most PHP frameworks follow MVC to separate concerns.
They include dependency injection and configuration via environment variables.
Use frameworks for larger apps to avoid reinventing authentication, routing, validation, etc.
Understand the fundamentals first; frameworks build on core PHP concepts.
summary: Laravel and Symfony are popular frameworks.
Frameworks commonly use MVC and dependency injection.
They speed up development for real apps.

details: REST APIs model resources (nouns) and use HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, DELETE).
Return consistent JSON responses and meaningful HTTP status codes.
Validate requests strictly and return clear error messages.
Use authentication (tokens/sessions) and enforce authorization checks per endpoint.
Document endpoints and version your API when making breaking changes.
summary: Use HTTP verbs to act on resources.
Validate input and handle errors cleanly.
